source.title: Breaking Bad Tokens: Detoxification of LLMs Using Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Agam Goyal; Vedant Rathi; W. Yeh; Yian Wang; Yuen Chen; Hari Sundaram

record.tranche_reason: The study tests SAE-recovered features in LLMs and reports that feature splitting in wider SAEs weakens detoxification, refining the claim that SAE features are stable, canonical units.
record.gate_note: The paper tests SAE features and their interventions in LLMs, including feature activity sparsity and a comparison of SAE widths. It does not test toy-model superposition geometry, feature competition for neuron capacity, neuron polysemanticity, or whether LLM features are distributed across neurons. Figure-based trends are included only where the accompanying text states the outcome; the text gives few exact toxicity scores for the main strength sweeps.
record.test_reason: This is mainly a detoxification-method paper that uses SAE features as a tool (T4 for most results). Its one result on the claim is the 16K vs 65K GemmaScope comparison (Section 4.4). There, toxic features split in the wider SAE and steering degrades. The authors take this to mean wider SAEs do not learn truly disentangled features, which bears on V5 (stable, canonical units). No toy-model, capacity, polysemanticity or feature-dimensionality results are reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add that the authors report SAE steering matching or beating DPO, LM-Steer, ProFS and prompting at higher strengths. They also report preserved LM-Harness benchmark accuracy, and fluency collapse in GPT-2 but not Gemma. They conclude that feature splitting in wider SAEs hampers safety interventions and that current wide SAEs are not truly disentangled.
record.recipe_differences: The study applies pretrained SAEs to residual-stream activations in GPT2 and Gemma, selects toxicity-associated features from paired toxic/non-toxic text, and ablates or steers their decoder vectors. It does not use the toy-model setup or measurements from the original superposition study.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with model, layer, SAE width, feature-selection method, steering strength, and whether steering is constant, conditional per-input, or conditional per-token.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating or steering along decoder vectors of selected toxicity SAE features reduces RealToxicityPrompts toxicity in GPT-2 Small, Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-2B-IT. Effects vary by layer, steering mode and strength; strong steering collapses GPT-2 fluency.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE-feature steering is an effective, capability-preserving detoxification method in small LLMs.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected toxicity SAE features are non-zero on under 0.5% of tokens.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Toxicity-selected SAE features are sparsely active.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: Only two base model families are studied, with a limited number of layers and manually selected toxicity features. Feature activity sparsity measurements cover only selected features. Many toxicity outcomes are given as qualitative descriptions or plotted trends rather than exact values; the paper reports no uncertainty for the principal intervention outcomes in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Fluency, benchmark capability, feature-knowledge retention, and toxicity-detector agreement were not catalogued because they do not measure the versions' claimed representational geometry or feature recovery.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, geometry or sparsity transition.
All: no test of capacity competition or of dedicated versus shared dimensions.
All: no measure of features spreading across neurons; no general test of sparse-feature recovery. Sparsity and steering are shown only for hand-picked features.
Completeness; stability across seeds, models or training runs. Canonicality is probed only via one width comparison with a downstream metric.
All: no test of feature dimensionality.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 support and limits_scope labels are dropped: the detox rows measure the study's own method performance, not superposition or feature recovery. The V5 evidence is indirect, based on downstream toxicity, and comes from one model and one width pair. R16 shows summing split features restores performance; it is linked to V5 but not labelled.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, overcomplete sparse-feature setting, near-orthogonal geometry, sparsity transition, or regular geometric arrangement are tested.
The study does not test whether features compete for neuron capacity or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
The study does not measure polysemantic neurons or test mechanisms that produce polysemanticity without capacity pressure.

It studies selected toxicity-related SAE features and their effects, not whether features generally spread across many neurons; evidence is limited to the tested models, layers, SAE widths, and toxicity setting.

The study reports feature splitting and width-dependent intervention outcomes, but does not assess whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical across tasks, models, or training conditions.
The study uses individual decoder vectors for interventions but does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features or test the dimensionality of represented features.

rows.subject: gemma-2-2b
rows.operation_detail: Compared constant steering using best-performing features from 16K and 65K GemmaScope SAEs.
rows.measure: Difference in average toxicity between SAE-width interventions
rows.baseline: 16K SAE steering
rows.value: Interventions using the 65K SAE had toxicity scores on average 0.062 higher across steering strengths and both layers
rows.note: The authors attribute the weaker outcome to feature splitting: individual toxic features fragmented across narrower definitions in the wider SAE.
rows.check: Stability across dictionary width is absent: features split and steering is 0.062 worse in toxicity. This is an indirect measure (downstream toxicity); the splitting itself is described, not quantified.

rows.subject: gemma-2-2b
rows.operation_detail: Steered with the sum of decoder vectors for the 65K SAE toxic features, scaled by their average steering factor.
rows.measure: Difference in average toxicity between width-based interventions
rows.baseline: Original 65K feature steering difference from 16K result: 0.062
rows.value: Composition-based steering reduced the difference to 0.01 while maintaining fluency
rows.note: This post-hoc approach made 65K nearly as effective as 16K for detoxification; it does not establish that the 65K feature dictionary is canonical or complete.
rows.check: Summing the split 65K features recovers 16K-level detox (gap 0.01). This is consistent with splitting but says nothing direct about canonicality.

relationships.condition: Gemma-2-2B GemmaScope residual SAEs, 16K vs 65K width, layers 10 and 20, toxicity features
relationships.reason: Toxic features split in the 65K SAE, and its best single-feature steering is 0.062 more toxic on average (R15). The authors state wider SAEs do not learn truly disentangled features.
relationships.display_finding: Toxic features split in the 65K SAE and its best single-feature steering was 0.062 more toxic on average; the authors state wider SAEs do not learn truly disentangled features.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Selected toxicity-related features in GPT2 Small, Gemma-2-2B, and Gemma-2-2B-IT
reader_labels.reason: Selected SAE features are sparsely active in the reported measurements and intervening on them reduces toxicity; see R1–R14 and R17–R26.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Feature selection, layer, steering mode, and SAE width
reader_labels.reason: Effectiveness varies by layer and steering mode, and the wider SAE yields weaker detoxification than the 16K SAE in the reported comparison; see R8–R16 and R22–R24.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports that features split in the wider SAE and its individual-feature interventions have toxicity scores 0.062 higher on average; see R15.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Combining decoder vectors for split features reduces the reported difference to 0.01, so the intervention problem is mitigable in this tested setting, but this does not demonstrate canonicality; see R16.
